collection.title: Serial dependence carries the action that produced the previous report (earlier version)
collection.authors: Qu, C.; Naeve, C.; Shi, Z.
collection.author_corresponding_institution: Neuro-Cognitive Psychology, Department of Psychology, LMU Munich
collection.abstract: Serial dependence pulls current judgments toward the recent past, but what is carried forward is debated: the previous stimulus, the previous decision, or something about the report itself. Three magnitude-reproduction experiments separated these sources. Participants viewed dot arrays that varied independently in duration and numerosity, then reproduced the cued dimension by holding a key while a display accumulated, so that both magnitudes were produced through the same action. A response-history model partitioned the attraction into previous-stimulus and previous-response paths. The previous response predicted cross-dimensional attraction after controlling for the previous and current stimuli: a numerosity report biased the next duration judgment and vice versa (Experiment 1), also when each task used its own response key (Experiment 2). A task switch weakened this carryover without abolishing it. Experiment 3 randomized, trial by trial, whether a reported number required a long or a short key hold. The influence of a previous number on the next duration judgment changed with this mapping, showing that reported value alone did not account for carryover. Conventional stimulus-based measures showed none of this cross-task history. Serial dependence can therefore carry the trace of the action through which a previous judgment was expressed, bounded but not gated by task context.

collection.title: Auditing Biomedical Literature with Blinded AI Peer Review: Where Peer Review Works, Where It Fails, and How to Strengthen It
collection.authors: Kosakovsky Pond, S. L.; Pond, S. J. K.; Weaver, S.; Zehr, J. D.; Martin, D. P.; Nekrutenko, A.
collection.author_corresponding_institution: Institute for Genomics and Evolutionary Medicine, Department of Biology, Temple University, Philadelphia, PA, USA
collection.abstract: Biomedical publishing has grown more than elevenfold since 1991, outstripping human peer review. Unblinded language models cannot audit this literature objectively because they recognize famous authors and journals from training memory. We built BARS (Blinded AI Review System), an automated referee that strips titles, author names, institutions, journal headers, and dates before grading full-text manuscripts on a 10-point scale covering methods, evidence, biology, and reproducibility. We used BARS to generate 1,874 blind reviews across 1,714 unique papers. BARS passed 100% of verified sound controls, caught 77% to 91% of internally flawed papers, eliminated a +0.35-point prestige boost, and more than doubled human referee consistency. Across 320 recent open-access articles (2020-2025) from eight fields, 54% failed on core scientific rigor (<5.0/10; 41% excluding megajournals). Revision at selective journals improved preprints more than twice as much as revision at commercial megajournals (+0.62 vs. +0.30 points; baseline-adjusted p = 0.033), and BARS recalled 98% of unresolved human referee critiques across 100 open-review papers. Across 915 date-blinded papers from 1991 to 2025, average scores fell from 7.6/10 to 5.8/10 as megajournals and template database studies expanded. Blinded self-audits of 238 papers by two senior authors -- and of this manuscript itself -- caught real statistical, control, and table errors in our own work. At four cents per paper, BARS offers a practical quality check for authors, journals, and readers (https://veg.github.io/BARS/).

collection.title: Conserved synaptic modifications by humanized tau through diverse isoform- and mutation-specific intracellular interactions
collection.authors: Nickerson, E.; Pomeroy-Tuck, J.; Pratt, S.; Rodriguez, C.; Zhao, T.; Stodola, T.; Hoffman, B.; Maser, R.; Bloss, E.
collection.abstract: Mutations in the microtubule-binding protein tau are considered causal for a diverse group of neurodegenerative diseases collectively referred to as primary tauopathies. Specific tauopathies are associated with different mutations, distinct tau isoforms, manifest in unique cellular and circuit-wide patterns of degeneration, and present with specific clinical symptoms and trajectories. The mechanisms that link variations in the primary tau protein structure to distinct forms of neural circuit dysfunction remain largely unknown. Here, we created an orthogonal viral resource to systematically examine the impact of expressing humanized tau isoforms harboring different disease-relevant mutations in excitatory pyramidal cells from the mouse prelimbic cortex. We used these reagents to show that expression of mutant humanized tau (hTau) as either of two isoforms produced very similar patterns of circuit-specific synaptic disconnection on cortical projection neurons. However, mass spectrometry revealed that the interactomes of these different tau species varied markedly as functions of isoform, mutation, and subcellular location. We validated the functional relevance of increased hTau interactions with mitochondrial proteins in induced neurons differentiated from Ngn2-iPSCs expressing different hTau constructs. These results suggest different disease-relevant hTau proteins likely use distinct mechanisms to drive a highly stereotyped form of synapse loss in cortical neurons.
